transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hi Dr. Smith. I've been having a really hard time lately because I just can't seem to stay in my seat when I'm supposed to, like during work meetings or meals. I feel this constant urge to get up and move around, and it's starting to cause some issues.
Do you also have trouble focusing or staying on task, such as during conversations or when reading?
I don't think I have much trouble focusing during conversations or when I'm reading. I'm not quite sure about that, as those specific things seem mostly okay to me.

{
  "category": "symptom duration",
  "subcategory": "hyperactivity",
  "question": "Have you felt this way since childhood, or did these symptoms start more recently?"

I've actually had these kinds of struggles since I was a kid, definitely before I turned 12. However, it has become a really consistent and disruptive problem for about the last year and eight months.

{
  "category": "differential point",
  "subcategory": "impulsivity",
  "question": "Do you often feel the need to interrupt others during conversations or have difficulty waiting your turn in activities or lines?"
I don't think I really have an issue with interrupting people during conversations. Waiting my turn in lines or during activities doesn't usually bother me either.
Has there been a specific stressful event or major life change around the time your symptoms became more disruptive, about a year and eight months ago?

I can't recall any specific stressful event or major life change happening around that time. However, I can confirm that these difficulties have indeed been going on and causing me consistent issues for about a year and eight months.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)", "Adjustment Disorder"], but Adjustment Disorder is now ruled out because the patient does not recall any specific stressful event or major life change around the time symptoms worsened, which is required for that diagnosis. The symptoms (persistent restlessness, inability to stay seated, onset in childhood, and duration over years) strongly support ADHD. The absence of significant impulsivity (no issues with interrupting or waiting turns) makes the predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation less typical, but the lifelong course and physical hyperactivity still best align with this subtype. No evidence of mood, anxiety, trauma, or psychotic disorders is present. Thus, the only remaining candidate is ADHD (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation), though atypical, as the core hyperactivity is clear and onset is developmental.
